clinicalPearls: Superficial fungal infections are caused by molds and yeasts that colonize the outer skin layers, hair follicles, and nails without invading deeper tissue; they are the most common human fungal infections but rarely cause serious disease.

Dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) are not part of normal skin flora and confine themselves to keratinized structures; symptoms arise from inflammatory reaction to fungal antigens rather than tissue invasion, and an estimated billion people are affected worldwide.

The annular, ring-shaped cutaneous lesion ('ringworm') results from centrifugal outward growth of the organism in the stratum corneum; the term tinea (Latin for worm) is preferred and is paired with the affected body site.
Tinea capitis predominantly affects children aged 3 to 7 years, producing well-demarcated scaly patches with hair shafts broken off near the skin surface and possible alopecia.

Tinea pedis typically begins in the toe web spaces with peeling, maceration, and pruritus, and is a recognized portal of entry for streptococci and staphylococci, predisposing to lower-extremity cellulitis through interdigital fissures.

Onychomycosis affects toenails more often than fingernails, is most common in those with tinea pedis, and shows thickened, discolored, crumbling nails with onycholysis; older age, vascular disease, diabetes, and nail trauma are risk factors.

Malassezia yeasts (notably M. furfur, M. pachydermatis) are lipophilic commensals of sebum-rich areas (back, chest, scalp, face) and cause tinea/pityriasis versicolor, folliculitis, and seborrheic dermatitis; cutaneous IL-17 signaling normally controls them.
Tinea versicolor appears as flat round scaly hypo- or hyperpigmented patches on the neck, chest, or upper arms, usually asymptomatic, and can be confused with vitiligo (which is non-scaly).

KOH (potassium hydroxide) preparation of lesion-edge scrapings demonstrating hyphae is the key bedside diagnostic test; Malassezia shows a characteristic mix of budding bottle-shaped yeasts and short septate hyphae.

Mucocutaneous candidiasis is most often caused by Candida albicans; oral thrush yields white mucosal plaques that scrape off, and antibiotic use, diabetes, and pregnancy are major risk factors for vulvovaginal candidiasis.

Candida auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant species that persistently colonizes human skin, hair follicles, healthcare environments, and devices, grows avidly in human sweat, and drives nosocomial outbreaks.

Seborrheic dermatitis (a Malassezia-associated condition) can be especially severe in patients with AIDS, and Malassezia fungemia, though rare, occurs almost exclusively in premature neonates receiving parenteral lipid nutrition.
harrison.pathophysiology: Superficial fungi inhabit only the keratinized superficial layers (stratum corneum, hair follicles, nail plate) and do not invade beneath the stratum corneum. Dermatophytes live within keratin and produce disease through host inflammatory responses to fungal antigens rather than by direct tissue invasion; nail involvement begins via the lateral or superficial nail plate then spreads, and hair-shaft invasion may be intra- or peri-shaft. Host defense is mediated by IL-17 responses, which restrict dermatophyte growth and control cutaneous Malassezia; infections are more frequent in males, and progesterone can inhibit dermatophyte growth. Malassezia organisms are lipophilic commensals of sebaceous areas that elicit little inflammation but, when IL-17 responses are excessive, can exacerbate atopic inflammation. Candida species are mucosal/cutaneous commensals; control depends on IL-17-producing lymphoid cells (TH17, gamma-delta T cells, innate lymphoid cells) at barrier sites, and defects in IL-17 signaling predispose to oral and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
additionalDifferentials: Psoriasis (can mimic both tinea corporis and onychomycosis)
Vitiligo (for tinea versicolor; differentiated by absence of scale)
infectionMimics: Oral leukoplakia from other infections vs Candida thrush
additionalInvestigations: KOH (potassium hydroxide) microscopy of scrapings from the lesion edge to detect hyphae
Fungal culture, indicated when an outbreak is suspected or when there is no response to therapy
KOH preparation showing budding bottle-shaped yeasts with short septate hyphae for Malassezia
Culture of Malassezia requires sterile olive oil added to the medium for suspected disseminated infection
Skin biopsy or nail clippings with culture and microscopy for skin and nail candidiasis

Biopsy of oral/esophageal tissue to distinguish invasive thrush (yeasts, pseudohyphae, and hyphae invading epithelium) from mere colonization (superficial yeast forms only) and from mimics such as leukoplakia
Culture and microscopy of vaginal secretions (swab) for vulvovaginal candidiasis
redFlags: Tinea pedis with interdigital fissuring predisposing to lower-extremity cellulitis from streptococcal/staphylococcal entry
Severe seborrheic dermatitis as a clue to AIDS / advanced immunosuppression
Malassezia fungemia/disseminated infection in premature neonates on parenteral lipid nutrition
Candida auris colonization as a nosocomial multidrug-resistant outbreak risk
Recurrent or extensive mucocutaneous candidiasis suggesting inborn errors of immunity (e.g., STAT1 gain-of-function, IL-17 signaling defects) or AIDS
Moderate-to-severe oral thrush or esophageal involvement requiring systemic evaluation
harrison.prognosis: Superficial fungal infections rarely cause serious disease. Malassezia skin infections are benign and self-limited, though recurrences are common. Dermatophyte infections generally respond well to therapy, but onychomycosis is slow to clear and prone to relapse. The outcome of rare systemic Malassezia infection depends on the host's underlying condition, though most affected neonates do well.
pitfalls: Diagnosing onychomycosis clinically without confirmation, since psoriasis can mimic nail fungal disease (usually with associated skin lesions)
Mistaking tinea versicolor for vitiligo; the absence of scale distinguishes vitiligo
Interpreting superficial yeast forms on oral/esophageal biopsy as invasive candidiasis when they actually represent colonization only
Overlooking tinea pedis as a portal for bacterial cellulitis
Not pursuing culture when a patient fails to respond to empiric therapy or when an outbreak is suspected
harrison.severityClassification: Clinically stratified by extent and site: localized cutaneous tinea versus extensive tinea and onychomycosis; for mucocutaneous candidiasis, mild oral thrush is distinguished from moderate/severe or esophageal disease that requires systemic management.
management: Treat cutaneous dermatophytosis such as tinea corporis, cruris and pedis with topical allylamine or azole antifungals
Use systemic antifungal therapy with terbinafine or an azole for onychomycosis and for tinea capitis, where topical treatment alone is inadequate
Manage Malassezia infections such as pityriasis versicolor with topical ketoconazole or selenium sulphide, reserving oral azoles for extensive disease
Keep affected skin dry and treat interdigital maceration to prevent bacterial cellulitis entering through toe-web fissures
Monitor liver function during prolonged oral terbinafine or azole courses and obtain fungal culture where there is no response to therapy
Advise on footwear hygiene, treatment of reservoirs and measures to reduce recurrence and reinfection
